codex.worst_flaw: The payout depends on recorded start times, but the design does not establish that those timestamps can reliably verify that checklists were completed before work began.

claude.worst_flaw: The design judges success with a single before/after company-wide comparison that has no control group and no costs or harms set in advance, so it cannot separate the reward's effect from paid time, app fixes and training introduced alongside it.

holistic.reason: Union-agreed, gaming-resistant, safety-first design with collective paid-time reward and sampling is approvable, but a one-hour team reward is modest and employees may barely notice it, while keeping paid completion time in the workflow and a four-week check gives decent durability.

codex.worst_flaw: Giving all technicians the bonus alongside paid checklist time, training, and reminders leaves no comparison group to show whether the bonus adds value.

claude.worst_flaw: The pilot covers all 300 technicians and judges success only by comparing results with the period before launch, so it cannot separate the bonus's effect from the paid time, reminder and offline fallback added at the same time, or from seasonal and case-mix changes. The all-or-nothing 90% threshold also gives no way back once a technician has missed too many jobs to qualify.

holistic.reason: Union-agreed, safety-conscious design with credit for stops, audits, fallback, and a retained reminder and paid time is approvable, but a one-time $50 bonus with a private-only view is a modest hook and durable change depends on the workflow fixes staying in place.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison group or prespecified decision criteria. Any rise in completion during the eight-week pilot can't be separated from the effects of offline sync fixes, the paid check time and novelty, so the design can't show whether the paid-time reward adds value over plain workflow support.

codex.worst_flaw: An ignored hazard can fall within the audit’s tolerated failure rate, allowing the payout and pilot to proceed without an immediate safety review.

holistic.reason: Collective, union-agreed, audit-backed design with equal credit for stops and kept enablers (paid check time, offline fallback) is strong, but the 1–2 hour pooled reward is small and weakly tied to individual effort, so salience and durability after the reward ends are only moderate.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison and no post-payout measurement. It judges success with a before/after on the team's own metrics and makes the continue/stop decision in a retrospective, so it cannot separate the reward's effect from the rotation and queue support or from normal variation.

codex.worst_flaw: A single report of rushed or after-hours review disqualifies the whole team for that week, giving engineers a reason to conceal the very harms the workload check is meant to detect.

holistic.reason: Unusually careful design with fair metrics, quality audits, workload safeguards and a team-level reward that suits sceptical engineers, but the two-hour prize is weak, the apparatus is heavy, and behaviour likely lapses once the queue, reminders and rotation end.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces the reward alongside the reviewer rotation and deadline feedback, so it cannot tell whether the reward adds any benefit.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design uses only a before/after comparison with a recalculated baseline, so it cannot separate the incentive from the rotation and plain deadline visibility. The single 90% team threshold also makes the reward all-or-nothing, and the design has no appeal process or replayable event and policy history for disputed clock decisions.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with capacity budgeting, quality audits and a team-level reward that suits sceptics, but the measurement and audit machinery is heavy for a 25-person team, a half-day reward is modest motivation, and lasting change depends on whether the rotation survives once the scorecard is retired.

claude.worst_flaw: The pilot has no comparison group or plain-feedback arm and no predefined success, cost or harm decision thresholds, so it can't separate the reward's effect from the rota and reminders, or from natural variation.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces the reward alongside protected review time, a rota, and reminders, so it cannot determine whether the reward adds value beyond those workflow changes.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, team-level, non-competitive and sceptic-friendly with protected time and audit safeguards, but the measurement and audit overhead is heavy, a two-hour reward is modest, and the habit may fade once the rota and reporting are retired.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot lacks a plain-feedback comparison, so any improvement could come from training, feedback, or kiosk fixes, leaving the ward award’s added value unknown.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no concurrent comparison wards or plain-support arm, so a before/after look at three wards cannot separate the incentive's effect from training, kiosk novelty or audit drift, and it never defines the decision rule or cost/harm thresholds for scaling.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with strong safeguards against gaming and clinical harm, but the audit-matching machinery is heavy to run and a one-time €300 team budget is a weak, low-salience motivator that likely fades once the pilot ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The award’s safety gate blocks launch because small audit samples and a five-point cutoff that ignores sampling uncertainty can let a ward qualify despite a material decline in hand-hygiene compliance.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no concurrent comparison ward or plain-feedback arm, and it changes kiosk workflow fixes, feedback and incentives all at once, so it cannot tell whether the €250 ward award adds anything beyond plain support.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, auditable, gaming-resistant and care-safe, but the €250 ward-level reward and matching admin burden are modest and complex, so engagement and post-incentive persistence of logging are uncertain.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no independent control or comparison against plain kiosk support and no baseline logging rate, and it has no staffed appeal or replayable event history. That leaves it unable to show that the incentive added value or to settle disputed matches fairly.

codex.worst_flaw: Without a plain-feedback comparison, the pilot cannot tell whether the ward reward improves verified logging beyond what training, access fixes, and feedback achieve.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with honest verification, safeguards against gaming and patient-safety pauses, but a $300 team fund and thank-yous are a weak motivator, the target is complex for nurses to grasp, and the habit likely fades once tracking and reward end.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot introduces the shared reward alongside workflow support and private feedback, so it cannot tell whether the reward adds value.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison group or isolation of incremental value. It judges success by a pre/post coverage change and a single four-week recheck, with no predefined decision rule, cost or sample consideration. It also never sets plain workflow support against the shared reward.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with audits, exceptions, quality guardrails and a sustainable end state, but the single team-wide 2-hour reward is weak and diffuse, the workflow is somewhat complex, and the 85% threshold sustained for two weeks may feel distant to agents starting at 12%.

codex.worst_flaw: Every queue receives the workflow changes and reward offer together, so the pilot cannot tell whether the reward improves coverage or quality beyond the workflow support alone.

claude.worst_flaw: It measures success only as a before/after change against a four-week baseline, with no comparison group or way to separate the incentive's effect from plain workflow support, and its single team-wide 90% target ignores differences in queue volume, case mix and each agent's feasible baseline.

holistic.reason: Rigorous measurement, audit and guardrails with a no-extra-pay reward that avoids crowding out, but a team-wide 90% threshold in two consecutive weeks from a 12% base is a very steep, brittle target that may demotivate and could easily go unearned, while the permanent close workflow and visible feedback give moderate durability.

codex.worst_flaw: The payout rule is a launch blocker because it requires 70% coverage across all resolved tickets without verifying that enough tickets have reusable guidance, creating pressure to attach irrelevant articles.

claude.worst_flaw: The design has no comparison group, plain-support arm or predefined decision rule, so a before/after rise in coverage cannot be credited to the incentive. It also has no replayable event history, shadow validation or staffed appeal process for disputed dispositions.

holistic.reason: Well-guarded design with quality sampling, CSAT/reopen gates, an exception path and a team-level reward that keeps the CSAT bonus intact, but the 2-hour learning-time reward is modest, the 70% target (from 12%) is a steep jump, and the team-wide threshold could feel remote and be gamed through generic links, so durability depends on the retained workflow and review rota.
